{{Short description|Mathematical spiral tiling}}
[[File:Voderberg-1.png|thumb|A partial Voderberg tiling. Note that all of the colored tiles are congruent.]]
'''Voderberg tiling''' is a mathematical [[spiral]] [[mathematical tiling|tiling]], invented in 1936 by mathematician {{ill|Heinz Voderberg|de}} (1911–1945).<ref name="mbook">{{cite book |last=Pickover |first=Clifford A. |date=2009 |title=The Math Book: From Pythagoras to the 57th Dimension, 250 Milestones in the History of Mathematics |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JrslMKTgSZwC |publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc. |page=372 |isbn=9781402757969 |access-date=24 March 2015 }}</ref> [[Karl Reinhardt (mathematician)|Karl August Reinhardt]] posed the question, "Is there a tile such that two copies can completely enclose a third copy?" Voderberg, his student, answered in the affirmative with {{Lang|de|Form eines Neunecks eine Lösung zu einem Problem von Reinhardt}} ["On a nonagon as a solution to a problem of Reinhardt"].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adams |first=Jadie |last2=Lopez |first2=Gabriel |last3=Mann |first3=Casey |last4=Tran |first4=Nhi |date=2020-03-14 |title=Your Friendly Neighborhood Voderberg Tile |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0025570X.2020.1708685 |journal=Mathematics Magazine |language=en |volume=93 |issue=2 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.1080/0025570X.2020.1708685 |issn=0025-570X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Karl Reinhardt - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Reinhardt/ |access-date=2023-07-09 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

Voderberg tiling is monohedral, consisting of a single shape that [[Tessellation|tessellates]] the plane with congruent copies of itself. In this case, the [[prototile]] is an elongated irregular [[nonagon]], or nine-sided figure. The most interesting feature of this [[polygon]] is the fact that two copies of it can fully enclose a third one. For example, the lowest purple nonagon is enclosed by two yellow ones, all three of identical shape.<ref name="voderberg">{{cite journal|author=Voderberg, Heinz |date=1936 |title=Zur Zerlegung der Umgebung eines ebenen Bereiches in kongruente |journal= Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung |url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN37721857X_0046?tify={%22pages%22:[235]} |volume=46|pages=229–231  }}</ref> Before Voderberg's discovery, mathematicians had questioned whether this could be possible.

Because it has no [[translational symmetries]], Voderberg tiling is technically [[aperiodic tiling|non-periodic]], even though it exhibits an obvious repeating pattern and its [[prototile]] can also be used to create a periodic tiling. 

Vorderberg tiling was the first spiral tiling to be devised,<ref name="special">{{cite web | url=https://www.uwgb.edu/dutchs/symmetry/radspir1.htm | title=Some Special Radial and Spiral Tilings | publisher=University of Wisconsin, Green Bay | date=29 July 1999 | access-date=24 March 2015 | author=Dutch, Steven | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305011416/https://www.uwgb.edu/dutchs/symmetry/radspir1.htm | archive-date=5 March 2016 | url-status=dead | df=dmy-all }}</ref> preceding later work by [[Branko Grünbaum]] and [[Geoffrey C. Shephard]] in the 1970s.<ref name="mbook" /> 

A spiral tiling is depicted on the cover of Grünbaum and Shephard's 1987 book ''[[Tilings and patterns]]''.<ref>{{citation
